sentences.t:
संन्यासस्य महाबाहो तत्त्वमिच्छामि वेदितुम् ।
त्यागस्य च हृषीकेश पृथक्केशिनिषूदन ॥
sentences.tr:
saṃnyāsasya mahā-bāho tattvam icchāmi veditum |
tyāgasya ca hṛṣīkeśa pṛthak keśiniṣūdana ||

morph.gloss: renunciation, relinquishment (from sam-ni-as, 'to lay/cast aside completely') (gen. sg. masc., 'of renunciation')
great (first member)
arm (mahā-bāho: 'great-armed one', vocative sg. masc., addressed to Kṛṣṇa)

sentences.l: Of renunciation, great-armed one, the truth I wish to know, to know, and of relinquishment, Lord-of-the-senses — separately, slayer-of-Keśin.
sentences.i: I want to know the truth about renunciation, great-armed one — and about relinquishment too, Hṛṣīkeśa — each taken separately, Keśiniṣūdana.
sentences.n: The final chapter opens with a question the poem has left hanging since 5.1-6, where saṃnyāsa and tyāga were already used without being formally distinguished: Arjuna now asks Kṛṣṇa to define each term pṛthak, 'separately, on its own'. Hṛṣīkeśa, 'lord of the senses', is a standing epithet of Kṛṣṇa; Keśiniṣūdana, 'slayer of Keśin', recalls the horse-demon Kṛṣṇa killed in his youth and is rare in the poem, appearing here as the chapter's opening address. Kṛṣṇa's answer, distinguishing the two terms technically, follows immediately in verse 2.

काम्यानां कर्मणां न्यासं संन्यासं कवयो विदुः ।
सर्वकर्मफलत्यागं प्राहुस्त्यागं विचक्षणाः ॥
sentences.tr:
kāmyānām karmaṇām nyāsam saṃnyāsam kavayaḥ viduḥ |
sarva-karma-phala-tyāgam prāhuḥ tyāgam vicakṣaṇāḥ ||

morph.gloss: done from desire, optional, motivated by a wish for reward (kāmyānām: gen. pl. neut., agreeing with karmaṇām)
action (gen. pl. neut., 'of actions')
a laying-down, a giving-up (acc. sg. masc., object of viduḥ)

a sage, a seer, a wise man (nom. pl. masc., subject; -aḥ before v- → -o)

sentences.l: The-laying-down of-desire-motivated actions, renunciation, the-wise know; the-giving-up-of-the-fruit-of-all-action, relinquishment, the-discerning call.
sentences.i: The wise call giving up desire-driven action 'renunciation'; the discerning call giving up the fruit of every action 'relinquishment'.
sentences.n: Kṛṣṇa opens with two technical definitions rather than a value judgment: saṃnyāsa is nyāsa, 'the laying-down', of kāmyāni karmāṇi, 'actions performed from desire' (optional rites undertaken for some reward); tyāga is specifically sarva-karma-phala-tyāga, 'giving up the fruit of all action', leaving the action itself in place. This distinction governs the whole chapter's argument through verse 12: outright abstention from action (implied by an unqualified saṃnyāsa) is set aside in favor of acting while relinquishing the fruit, the teaching already given at 2.47-51 and repeated through chapters 3-6. Kavayaḥ, 'the wise, the seers', and vicakṣaṇāḥ, 'the discerning', are near-synonyms naming authorities on each side of the definition, not two rival schools.

यज्ञदानतपःकर्म न त्याज्यमिति चापरे ॥

sentences.l: 'To-be-abandoned, as-faulty' — thus some, action, declare, the-wise; 'the-action-of-sacrifice-giving-and-austerity is not to-be-abandoned' — thus others.
sentences.i: Some wise men hold that action should be given up as inherently flawed; others say that sacrifice, giving, and austerity should not be given up.
sentences.n: A three-verse survey of rival views on renunciation precedes Kṛṣṇa's own verdict at verse 5: eke, 'some', judge all karma doṣavat, 'faulty' (because action inevitably entangles its agent, the very problem the chapter returns to at verses 59-60), and so counsel giving it up outright; apare, 'others', exempt yajña-dāna-tapas, 'sacrifice, giving and austerity', holding these three obligatory regardless. Manīṣiṇaḥ, 'thoughtful men, sages', echoes kavayaḥ/vicakṣaṇāḥ of verse 2.

sentences.t:
निश्चयं शृणु मे तत्र त्यागे भरतसत्तम ।
त्यागो हि पुरुषव्याघ्र त्रिविधः संप्रकीर्तितः ॥
sentences.tr:
niścayam śṛṇu me tatra tyāge bharata-sattama |
tyāgaḥ hi puruṣa-vyāghra trividhaḥ saṃprakīrtitaḥ ||

morph.gloss: determination, settled conclusion, verdict (niścaya: acc. sg. masc., object of śṛṇu)
to hear (śṛṇu: imperative 2nd sg., 'hear!')
I (me: gen. sg., 'my')
there, on that point, in that regard (adverb)
relinquishment (loc. sg., 'concerning relinquishment')
descendant of Bharata (first member)
best (bharata-sattama: 'best of the Bharatas', vocative, addressed to Arjuna)
relinquishment (nom. sg. masc., subject; -aḥ before h- → -o)
for, indeed (particle)
man (first member)
tiger (puruṣa-vyāghra: 'tiger among men', vocative, addressed to Arjuna)
threefold (nom. sg. masc., predicate)
to proclaim, declare (saṃprakīrtita: past participle; nom. sg. masc., predicate, 'is proclaimed')

sentences.l: The-verdict hear from-me on-that, on-relinquishment, best-of-the-Bharatas: relinquishment, for, tiger-among-men, threefold [is] proclaimed.
sentences.i: Hear my settled conclusion on relinquishment, best of the Bharatas: relinquishment, tiger among men, is said to be of three kinds.
sentences.n: Kṛṣṇa sets aside the rival views just surveyed to give his own niścaya, 'settled conclusion, verdict' — a word marking this as the poem's authoritative resolution rather than one more opinion. Bharata-sattama and puruṣa-vyāghra, 'best of the Bharatas' and 'tiger among men', are both epithets of Arjuna. The threefold classification of tyāga announced here is unpacked in verses 7-9 (tāmasa, rājasa, sāttvika tyāga), the first of the guṇa-triads structuring the rest of the chapter.

sentences.t:
यज्ञदानतपःकर्म न त्याज्यं कार्यमेव तत् ।
यज्ञो दानं तपश्चैव पावनानि मनीषिणाम् ॥
sentences.tr:
yajña-dāna-tapaḥ-karma na tyājyam kāryam eva tat |
yajñaḥ dānam tapaḥ ca eva pāvanāni manīṣiṇām ||

morph.gloss: sacrifice (first member)
giving (second member)
austerity (third member)
action (yajña-dāna-tapaḥ-karma: 'the action of sacrifice, giving and austerity', nom. sg. neut., subject)
not
to abandon (tyājya: gerundive; nom. sg. neut., predicate)
to do (kārya: gerundive, 'is to be done'; kāryam: nom. sg. neut., predicate; simply joined with eva, final -m unaffected before the vowel)
indeed, precisely

sacrifice (nom. sg. masc., subject; -aḥ before d- → -o)
giving (nom. sg. neut., subject)
austerity (tapaḥ: nom. sg. neut., subject; -aḥ+c- → -aś c-)
and
indeed (ca+eva → caiva, a+e → ai)

a thoughtful man, a sage (gen. pl., 'for the wise')

sentences.l: The-action-of-sacrifice-giving-and-austerity not to-be-abandoned; to-be-done indeed, that. Sacrifice, giving, and-indeed austerity, [are] purifying, for-the-wise.
sentences.i: The acts of sacrifice, giving, and austerity are not to be given up — they are indeed to be performed: sacrifice, giving, and austerity are purifying, even for the wise.
sentences.n: Kṛṣṇa states his own position on the disagreement just surveyed: sacrifice, giving and austerity remain kāryam eva, 'indeed to be performed', because they are pāvanāni, 'purifying', even for manīṣiṇām, 'the wise' — who, on the extreme view of verse 3, might be thought to have outgrown the need for them. This settles what, if anything, is to be given up outright, before verse 6 explains how the three should be practiced.

sentences.t:
एतान्यपि तु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा फलानि च ।
कर्तव्यानीति मे पार्थ निश्चितं मतमुत्तमम् ॥
sentences.tr:
etāni api tu karmāṇi saṅgam tyaktvā phalāni ca |
kartavyāni iti me pārtha niścitam matam uttamam ||

morph.gloss: these (etāni: nom. pl. neut., resuming yajña-dāna-tapaḥ-karma of verse 5; etāni+api → etānyapi, -i+a- → -y a-)
even, indeed
but, however
action (nom. pl. neut., in apposition to etāni)

to abandon (tyaktvā: gerund, 'having abandoned')
fruit (acc. pl. neut., second object of tyaktvā)
and
to do (kartavya: gerundive, 'are to be done'; kartavyāni: nom. pl. neut., predicate agreeing with etāni karmāṇi; kartavyāni+iti → kartavyānīti, i+i → ī)
thus (closing the quoted view)
I (me: gen. sg., 'my')
son of Pṛthā, Arjuna (vocative)
determined, settled, definite (niścita: past participle; nom. sg. neut., predicate agreeing with matam)
opinion, view (mata: nom. sg. neut., subject; simply joined with uttamam, final -m unaffected before the vowel)

sentences.l: These indeed, however, actions, attachment having-abandoned, and-[their]-fruits, are-to-be-done — thus [is] my, Pārtha, settled opinion, the-best.
sentences.i: But these very actions should be performed, with attachment and their fruits given up — this, Pārtha, is my settled and highest view.
sentences.n: Closes the opening definitional section (verses 2-6): even the obligatory rites just named must be performed with saṅgam ... phalāni ca tyaktvā, 'attachment and their fruits given up' — restating tyāga in verse 2's technical sense (phala-tyāga) as the correct practice, against outright abstention. Niścitam ... matam uttamam, 'my settled and highest opinion', echoes niścayam of verse 4, marking Kṛṣṇa's final word on the question that opened the chapter before he turns, in verses 7-12, to classify tyāga itself by guṇa.

sentences.t:
नियतस्य तु संन्यासः कर्मणो नोपपद्यते ।
मोहात्तस्य परित्यागस्तामसः परिकीर्तितः ॥
sentences.tr:
niyatasya tu saṃnyāsaḥ karmaṇaḥ na upapadyate |
mohāt tasya parityāgaḥ tāmasaḥ parikīrtitaḥ ||

morph.gloss: prescribed, fixed, obligatory (niyata: past participle; gen. sg. neut., agreeing with karmaṇaḥ)
but
renunciation (nom. sg. masc., subject)
action (gen. sg. neut., 'of action'; -aḥ before n- → -o)
not (na+upapadyate → nopapadyate, a+u → o)
to be fitting, to apply, to be proper (upapadyate: present middle 3rd sg.)

it, its (tasya: gen. sg., referring back to niyatasya karmaṇaḥ)
abandonment, relinquishment (parityāgaḥ: nom. sg. masc., subject; -aḥ+t- → -as t-)

to proclaim, declare (parikīrtita: past participle; nom. sg. masc., predicate, 'is proclaimed')

sentences.l: Of-prescribed action, however, renunciation not is-fitting; out-of-delusion, its abandonment, tamas-natured, [is] proclaimed.
sentences.i: But renunciation of one's prescribed duty is not proper; giving it up out of delusion is declared to be tamas-natured.
sentences.n: Opens the tyāga-triad promised at verse 4 (vv. 7-9). Niyatasya karmaṇaḥ saṃnyāsaḥ na upapadyate, 'renunciation of prescribed action is not proper', rejects outright abandonment of one's obligatory duty as such — the same argument chapter 3 already made against total inaction (3.4-8). Mohāt, 'out of delusion', names the motive that makes such abandonment tāmasaḥ, tamas-natured: mistaking the duty itself for a fault, rather than only its fruit.

स कृत्वा राजसं त्यागं नैव त्यागफलं लभेत् ॥

sentences.l: '[It is] painful' — merely thus, whatever action, out-of-fear-of-bodily-affliction, one-should-abandon, he, having-performed rajas-natured relinquishment, not-at-all the-fruit-of-relinquishment would-obtain.
sentences.i: If a person gives up some action simply because it is painful, from fear of bodily hardship, he has practiced relinquishment as rajas-natured, and will not gain the fruit of relinquishment at all.
sentences.n: The rajas-natured form of tyāga: giving up an action duḥkham iti eva, 'merely because it is painful', out of kāya-kleśa-bhayāt, 'fear of bodily hardship' — avoidance from discomfort rather than understanding — wins none of the tyāga-phalam, 'fruit of relinquishment', named again at verse 12.

sentences.l: '[It] is-to-be-done' — merely thus, whatever prescribed action is-performed, Arjuna, attachment having-given-up and-indeed [its] fruit, that relinquishment [is] held sattva-natured.
sentences.i: But when a person performs his prescribed action simply because it must be done, Arjuna, giving up attachment and its fruit — that relinquishment is held to be sattva-natured.
sentences.n: The sattva-natured form of tyāga: performing niyataṃ karma, 'prescribed action', for no reason but kāryam iti eva, 'because it is simply to be done', while giving up saṅgam ... phalam, 'attachment and the fruit' — the same formula used for sattva-natured sacrifice, austerity and giving throughout chapter 17 (yaṣṭavyam eva iti, dātavyam iti). This is the chapter's positive resolution of the opening debate: not saṃnyāsa (abandoning the action) but this kind of tyāga (abandoning only attachment to its fruit) is truly sattva-natured.

sentences.l: Not he-hates unpleasant action, to-the-pleasant not-he-clings — the-renouncer, imbued-with-sattva, intelligent, whose-doubt-is-cut-away,
sentences.i: A renouncer who neither hates disagreeable action nor clings to agreeable action, filled with sattva, intelligent, his doubts cut away —
sentences.n: A portrait of the sāttvika tyāgī: freedom from dveṣa toward disagreeable duty and from attachment (here read into kuśale na anuṣajjate) toward agreeable duty is what verse 9's ideal looks like in a person, echoing the poem's recurring rāga-dveṣa pairing (3.34, 7.27). Sattva-samāviṣṭaḥ, 'imbued with sattva', and chinna-saṃśayaḥ, 'his doubt cut away' (recalling 4.42's chittvainaṃ saṃśayam), describe the settled clarity such a person has reached; the sentence continues without a break into verse 11.

sentences.t:
न हि देहभृता शक्यं त्यक्तुं कर्माण्यशेषतः ।
यस्तु कर्मफलत्यागी स त्यागीत्यभिधीयते ॥

sentences.i: It is not possible for an embodied being to give up action altogether; but whoever gives up the fruit of action is the one truly called a renouncer.
sentences.n: A direct restatement, for the agent's own case, of the impossibility of total inaction already argued at 3.5-8: deha-bhṛtā, 'by an embodied being', it simply is not possible to give up action aśeṣataḥ, 'entirely, without remainder'. The only tyāga actually available — and so the only one deserving the name tyāgī — is karma-phala-tyāgī, 'one who relinquishes the fruit of action', the chapter's technical definition from verse 2 now confirmed as the sole workable form of renunciation.

sentences.l: Undesired, desired, and mixed — threefold [is] the-fruit of-action; it-comes-about, hereafter, for-non-renouncers; but not at-all for-renouncers.
sentences.i: The fruit of action is of three kinds — unwanted, wanted, and mixed — and it comes, after death, to those who have not relinquished it; but never to those who have.
sentences.n: Closes the tyāga-section (verses 7-12) by naming what true renunciation wins: ordinary action ripens into aniṣṭam, iṣṭam or miśram phalam, 'bad, good, or mixed fruit', binding a-tyāginām, 'those who do not relinquish [the fruit]', to a future birth (pretya, 'hereafter'), but it does not touch saṃnyāsinām here — meaning those who practice the phala-tyāga just defined, not literal abstainers from action.

सांख्ये कृतान्ते प्रोक्तानि सिद्धये सर्वकर्मणाम् ॥

sentences.l: These-five, great-armed-one, causes, learn from-me: in-Sāṃkhya, in-the-doctrine-of-final-conclusion, [they are] declared, for-the-accomplishment of-all-actions.
sentences.i: Learn from me, great-armed one, these five causes taught in Sāṃkhya, the doctrine that traces every act to its conclusion, as necessary for the accomplishment of any action.
sentences.n: Opens the chapter's analysis of action's structure (verses 13-19), preparing the ground for the knowledge/action/agent triads of verses 20-28. Sāṃkhye kṛtānte, 'in Sāṃkhya, the doctrine of final conclusions' — kṛtānta, elsewhere 'ordinance, decree', names Sāṃkhya's method of tracing every act back to its complete set of causes. Sāṃkhya is kept untranslated per convention, as at 2.39, 3.3; the five kāraṇāni, 'causes', are enumerated in verse 14.

विविधाश्च पृथक्चेष्टा दैवं चैवात्र पञ्चमम् ॥

sentences.l: The-seat, likewise the-agent, and the-instrument of-various-kinds, and various distinct-efforts, and-indeed here, fate, the-fifth.
sentences.i: The body that is action's seat, the agent, the instrument in its many forms, effort in its many kinds, and, fifth, fate.
sentences.n: Names the five kāraṇāni promised in verse 13, the traditional analysis of any completed act: adhiṣṭhāna, 'the seat, the substrate' (the psychophysical body in which action occurs); kartā, 'the agent'; karaṇam pṛthagvidham, 'the instrument, of various kinds' (the sense- and action-organs); vividhāḥ pṛthak ceṣṭāḥ, 'various distinct efforts' (the different exertions accompanying an act); and daivam, 'fate, the divine [factor]' — the element beyond the agent's own control. Verses 15-16 draw the conclusion that no one of these, least of all the self alone, should be mistaken for the sole doer.

sentences.i: Whatever action a man undertakes, with body, speech, or mind, whether right or wrong, these five are its causes.
sentences.n: Applies the fivefold analysis of verse 14 to any and every act: śarīra-vāṅ-manobhiḥ, 'by body, speech and mind', names the poem's standard threefold instrument of action (cf. the threefold tapas of 17.14-16); nyāyyam vā viparītam vā, 'whether right or wrong', makes clear the analysis holds regardless of the act's moral quality — a structural claim about causation whose ethical payoff follows in verse 16.

sentences.l: This being-so, however, who sees the-self alone as-the-agent — because-of-[his]-uncultivated-understanding, he does not [truly] see, the-dull-witted-one.
sentences.i: This being so, whoever regards the self alone as the agent, because his understanding is untrained, does not really see; he is dull-witted.
sentences.n: Draws the ethical conclusion from the fivefold analysis: given that any action has five contributing causes, one who sees the ātman kevalam, 'the self alone', as kartā, 'the agent', has failed to see correctly, owing to akṛta-buddhitvāt, 'an uncultivated understanding' (buddhi not yet properly trained, echoing kṛtānte of verse 13). Durmatiḥ, 'dull-witted, of perverse judgment', corrects a possible misreading of the poem's own teaching that the self does not act (13.29-31, 5.13-14): that teaching does not mean the self alone should be credited or blamed for worldly action, which always involves the other four causes too.

sentences.l: Whose sense-of-'I' is not ego-made, whose understanding is not tainted — even having-killed, he does not kill these people, and is not bound.
sentences.i: Whoever's sense of self is free of egoism, whose understanding is untainted — even in killing, he does not kill, and he is not bound.
sentences.n: The description of the true knower continues with a positive counterpart to verse 16: one whose bhāvaḥ, 'inner disposition, sense of self', is na ahaṃ-kṛtaḥ, 'not made of ego' (the false identification of self with doer, now shed), and whose buddhi, 'understanding', na lipyate, 'is not tainted' (by the results of action, cf. 5.7, 13.31), even hatvā api, 'even having killed' — recalling the argument of chapter 2 that the true self can neither kill nor be killed (2.19-21) — na hanti, 'does not [truly] kill', na nibadhyate, 'is not bound'. The line answers, from the far side of the teaching, Arjuna's original horror at killing his kinsmen in chapter 1.

sentences.t:

sentences.l: Knowledge, the-known, the-knower — threefold [is] the-impulse-to-action; the-instrument, the-action, the-agent — thus, threefold [is] the-compendium-of-action.
sentences.i: Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower — these three set action in motion; the instrument, the action, and the agent — these three together make up action complete.
sentences.n: Opens the chapter's central analytic passage (verses 18-19), pairing two triads: karma-codanā, 'what impels to action' (jñāna, jñeya, parijñātā — knowledge, the known, the knower), and karma-saṃgraha, 'the [full] compendium of action' (karaṇa, karma, kartā — instrument, action, agent). Of these six, jñāna, karma and kartā are each divided threefold by guṇa in what follows (verses 20-28); jñeya and parijñātā are not further subdivided. This verse supplies the vocabulary the rest of the section works through.

sentences.i: Knowledge, action, and the agent are each declared threefold too, according to the division of the guṇas, in this analysis by guṇa — hear these as well, just as they truly are.
sentences.n: Announces the three guṇa-triads structuring verses 20-28: jñāna (20-22), karma (23-25), and kartā (26-28), each divided sāttvika/rājasa/tāmasa — the same method chapter 17 applied to faith, worship, food, sacrifice, austerity and giving, now turned on the structure of action just named in verse 18. Guṇa-saṃkhyāne, 'in the enumeration by guṇa', is a common-noun use of saṃkhyāna, 'reckoning, analysis', distinct from (though wordplay on) the proper name Sāṃkhya of verse 13. Yathāvat, 'exactly as it is', promises precision in what follows.

sentences.l: By-which one beholds one imperishable essence in-all-beings, undivided among-things-divided — know that knowledge sattva-natured.
sentences.i: The knowledge by which a person sees one undying reality in all beings, undivided within things divided — know that to be sattva-natured knowledge.
sentences.n: Opens the jñāna-triad (verses 20-22). Ekaṃ bhāvam avyayam, 'one imperishable essence', names the single, changeless reality perceived within sarva-bhūteṣu ... vibhakteṣu, 'all beings ... things divided' — the one self or brahman seen underlying the apparent multiplicity of embodied beings, the poem's recurring vision of unity-in-diversity (cf. 6.29-30, 13.27-28). Avibhaktaṃ vibhakteṣu, 'undivided among the divided', is the verse's central paradox: the object of sāttvika knowledge does not itself fragment even though the bodies it inhabits are many.

sentences.n: The rajas-natured counterpart to verse 20: pṛthaktvena, 'through separateness', vetti nānā-bhāvān pṛthag-vidhān, 'perceives manifold distinct entities' — knowledge that stops at the plurality of individual beings without discerning the underlying unity, mistaking the many divided forms for many separate realities.

अतत्त्वार्थवदल्पं च तत्तामसमुदाहृतम् ॥
sentences.tr:
yat tu kṛtsna-vat ekasmin kārye saktam ahaitukam |
a-tattva-artha-vat alpam ca tat tāmasam udāhṛtam ||

morph.gloss: which (yat: nom. sg. neut. relative, subject)
but (dental+dental, written joined)
whole, entire (first member)
suffix 'like, as if' (kṛtsna-vat: 'as if [it were] the whole', adverb)
one (ekasmin: loc. sg. masc.)
an object, a task, an effect (kārye: loc. sg. neut., 'in one single object'; kṛtsnavat+ekasmin → kṛtsnavadekasmin, -t+e- → -d e-)
clinging, attached (sakta: past participle; nom. sg. neut., agreeing with jñānam understood)
without cause, groundless (ahaitukam: nom. sg. neut., predicate; simply joined, final -m unaffected before the vowel)
not [grasping] the real truth, the true meaning (first compound)
suffix 'having the nature of' (a-tattva-artha-vat: 'without any grasp of the real truth', nom. sg. neut., predicate; atattvārthavat+alpam → atattvārthavadalpam, -t+a- → -d a-)
trifling, petty, small (alpam: nom. sg. neut., predicate)
and
that (tat: nom. sg. neut., subject)
tamas-natured (tāmasam: nom. sg. neut., predicate; simply joined, final -m unaffected before the vowel)
to declare, state (udāhṛta: past participle; nom. sg. neut., predicate)

sentences.l: But which, as-if-the-whole in-one-single-object, clinging, without-cause, without-grasp-of-the-real-truth, and trifling — that [is] declared tamas-natured.
sentences.i: But knowledge that clings to a single thing as if it were everything, without reason, without any grasp of the truth, and petty — that is declared tamas-natured.
sentences.n: Closes the jñāna-triad. Kṛtsnavat ekasmin kārye saktam, 'clinging to one single object as if it were the whole', names knowledge trapped at the narrowest possible scope, against verse 20's vision of the one in the many and verse 21's grasp at least of the many themselves. Ahaitukam, 'without cause or reason', and a-tattva-artha-vat alpam, 'without grasp of the true reality, and trifling', complete the triad by naming its lowest form as one that neither reasons nor sees truly nor amounts to much.

sentences.t:
नियतं सङ्गरहितमरागद्वेषतः कृतम् ।
अफलप्रेप्सुना कर्म यत्तत्सात्त्विकमुच्यते ॥
sentences.tr:
niyatam saṅga-rahitam a-rāga-dveṣataḥ kṛtam |
a-phala-prepsunā karma yat tat sāttvikam ucyate ||

morph.gloss: prescribed, obligatory (niyata: past participle; nom. sg. neut., agreeing with karma)
attachment (first member)
free from, devoid of (saṅga-rahitam: 'free from attachment', nom. sg. neut., agreeing with karma; simply joined with the following word, final -m unaffected before the vowel)
freedom from attraction and aversion (a-rāga-dveṣataḥ: ablative-adverbial in -taḥ, 'out of freedom from attraction and aversion')
to do (kṛta: past participle; nom. sg. neut., agreeing with karma)
fruitless, without regard for the fruit (first member)
desirous of obtaining (desiderative adj. from āp; a-phala-prepsunā: 'by one not desiring the fruit', instr. sg. masc., agent)
action (nom. sg. neut., subject)
which (yat: nom. sg. neut. relative)
that (tat: nom. sg. neut., correlative; dental+dental, written joined)
sattva-natured (sāttvikam: nom. sg. neut., predicate; simply joined with tat, no change)
to say (ucyate: present passive 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: Prescribed, free-from-attachment, done without-attraction-or-aversion, by-one-not-desiring-the-fruit — the action which [is such], that is called sattva-natured.
sentences.i: Action that is prescribed, free from attachment, performed without attraction or aversion, by one who does not desire its fruit — that is called sattva-natured.
sentences.n: Opens the karma-triad (verses 23-25), recapitulating the definition of sāttvika tyāga already given at verse 9 and echoing 17.11's aphala-ākāṅkṣibhiḥ: niyatam, 'prescribed' (one's own duty, not chosen from desire); saṅga-rahitam, 'free from attachment'; arāga-dveṣataḥ kṛtam, 'done without attraction or aversion' (the same rāga-dveṣa pairing as verse 10); a-phala-prepsunā, 'by one not desiring the fruit' — together defining action performed exactly as chapters 2-3's core teaching requires.

sentences.t:
यत्तु कामेप्सुना कर्म साहंकारेण वा पुनः ।
क्रियते बहुलायासं तद्राजसमुदाहृतम् ॥
sentences.tr:
yat tu kāma-īpsunā karma sa-ahaṃkāreṇa vā punaḥ |
kriyate bahula-āyāsam tat rājasam udāhṛtam ||

morph.gloss: which (yat: nom. sg. neut. relative, subject)
but (dental+dental, written joined)
desire (first member)
desirous of obtaining (desiderative adj. from āp; kāma-īpsunā: 'by one craving [the fruit driven by] desire', instr. sg. masc.; kāma+īpsunā → kāmepsunā, a+ī → e, guṇa)
action (nom. sg. neut., subject)
with, together with (prefix)
egotism, the sense of 'I' (sa-ahaṃkāreṇa: 'with egotism', instr. sg.; sa+ahaṃkāreṇa → sāhaṃkāreṇa, a+a → ā)
or
again, further (punaḥ: its pausa form)
to do (kriyate: present passive 3rd sg.)
much, abundant (first member)
effort, exertion, toil (bahula-āyāsam: 'with much exertion', acc. sg. neut. used adverbially; bahula+āyāsam → bahulāyāsam, a+ā → ā)
that (tat: nom. sg. neut., subject; tat+rājasam → tadrājasam, -t+r- → -d r-)
rajas-natured (rājasam: nom. sg. neut., predicate)
to declare (udāhṛta: past participle; nom. sg. neut., predicate)

sentences.l: But the action which, by-one-craving-the-fruit-of-desire, or again with-egotism, is-performed with-much-exertion — that [is] declared rajas-natured.
sentences.i: But action performed by one driven by desire for its fruit, or again out of egotism, and carried out with great exertion — that is declared rajas-natured.
sentences.n: The rajas-natured counterpart: kāma-īpsunā, 'craving [the fruit that satisfies] desire', directly opposes verse 23's a-phala-prepsunā; sa-ahaṃkāreṇa, 'with egotism', names the 'I-am-the-doer' pride already condemned at 3.27; bahula-āyāsam, 'with much exertion', marks such action as effortful and grasping rather than calm.

sentences.t:
अनुबन्धं क्षयं हिंसामनवेक्ष्य च पौरुषम् ।
मोहादारभ्यते कर्म यत्तत्तामसमुच्यते ॥
sentences.tr:
anubandham kṣayam hiṃsām anavekṣya ca pauruṣam |
mohāt ārabhyate karma yat tat tāmasam ucyate ||

morph.gloss: consequence, subsequent entanglement (anubandha: acc. sg. masc., object of anavekṣya)
loss, decline, ruin (acc. sg. masc., object)
harm, injury (hiṃsām: acc. sg. fem., object)

not having considered, without regard for (anavekṣya: gerund with negative prefix; simply joined, final -m unaffected before the vowel — the vulgate reading, printed here; the BORI critical edition reads anapekṣya, 'without regard for' (an-apa-īkṣ), a close synonym from a different preverb: a real vulgate/BORI variant, not a misprint; see the note)
and
[one's own] capability, manly power, ability (acc. sg. neut., third object of anavekṣya)
delusion (mohāt: abl. sg., 'out of delusion')
to undertake, begin (ārabhyate: present passive 3rd sg.; mohāt+ārabhyate → mohādārabhyate, -t+ā- → -d ā-)
action (nom. sg. neut., subject)
which (yat: nom. sg. neut. relative)
that (tat: nom. sg. neut., correlative; yat+tat, dental+dental, written joined)
tamas-natured (tāmasam: nom. sg. neut., predicate; simply joined with tat)
to say (ucyate: present passive 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: Consequence, loss, harm, without-regard, and [one's-own] capability — the action which, out-of-delusion, is-undertaken, that is called tamas-natured.
sentences.i: Action undertaken out of delusion, with no regard for consequence, loss, harm, or one's own capacity — that is called tamas-natured.
sentences.n: Closes the karma-triad. Vulgate reads anavekṣya, 'without regard for, without having considered' (an-ava-īkṣ); the BORI critical edition reads anapekṣya, 'without regard for, disregarding' (an-apa-īkṣ), a close synonym from a different preverb — a real vulgate/BORI variant, not adopted here but noted. Anubandham, 'consequence, entanglement', kṣayam, 'loss, ruin', hiṃsām, 'harm [to others]', and pauruṣam, 'one's own strength or capability' are four things the tāmasa agent, acting mohāt, 'out of delusion', simply fails to weigh — the polar opposite of verse 23's carefully considered action.

sentences.t:
मुक्तसङ्गोऽनहंवादी धृत्युत्साहसमन्वितः ।
सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योर्निर्विकारः कर्ता सात्त्विक उच्यते ॥
sentences.tr:
mukta-saṅgaḥ an-ahaṃ-vādī dhṛti-utsāha-samanvitaḥ |
siddhi-asiddhyoḥ nirvikāraḥ kartā sāttvikaḥ ucyate ||

morph.gloss: freed, released (past participle of muc; first member)
attachment (mukta-saṅgaḥ: 'free from attachment', nom. sg. masc., predicate; -aḥ+a- → -o' with avagraha)
not asserting 'I', free from egotistical self-assertion (an-ahaṃ-vādī: nom. sg. masc., predicate)
steadfastness, firmness, resolve (first member)
energy, zeal, enthusiasm (second member; dhṛti+utsāha → dhṛtyutsāha, i+u → yu, yaṇ)
endowed with, possessed of (dhṛti-utsāha-samanvitaḥ: 'endowed with steadfastness and zeal', nom. sg. masc., predicate)
success (first item)
failure (siddhi-asiddhyoḥ: 'in success and failure', loc. dual; siddhi+asiddhyoḥ → siddhyasiddhyoḥ, i+a → ya, yaṇ)
unchanging, unaffected (nirvikāraḥ: nom. sg. masc., predicate; -oḥ+n- → -or n-)
the agent, the doer (nom. sg. masc., subject)
sattva-natured (nom. sg. masc., predicate; its visarga elided before the vowel u- of ucyate, hiatus retained — an accepted epic-verse option, already flagged at 17.14, 17.15)
to say (ucyate: present passive 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: Free-from-attachment, not-given-to-saying-'I', endowed-with-steadfastness-and-zeal, unaffected-in-success-and-failure — [such an] agent is-called sattva-natured.
sentences.i: An agent who is free from attachment, does not boast of himself, is full of resolve and zeal, and is unmoved by success or failure — such an agent is called sattva-natured.
sentences.n: Opens the kartā-triad (verses 26-28), the third and final triad promised at verse 19. Mukta-saṅgaḥ, 'free from attachment', an-ahaṃ-vādī, 'not asserting "I [am the doer]"', directly answers the ego-driven agent condemned at verses 16-17 and 24; dhṛti-utsāha-samanvitaḥ, 'endowed with steadfastness and zeal' (dhṛti anticipates its own triad at verses 33-35), and nirvikāraḥ siddhi-asiddhyoḥ, 'unmoved in success and failure', recall 2.48's samatvaṃ yoga ucyate. Its visarga is elided with hiatus kept before ucyate, an accepted epic option already seen at 17.14-15.

sentences.t:
रागी कर्मफलप्रेप्सुर्लुब्धो हिंसात्मकोऽशुचिः ।
हर्षशोकान्वितः कर्ता राजसः परिकीर्तितः ॥
sentences.tr:
rāgī karma-phala-prepsuḥ lubdhaḥ hiṃsā-ātmakaḥ a-śuciḥ |
harṣa-śoka-anvitaḥ kartā rājasaḥ parikīrtitaḥ ||

morph.gloss: passionate, full of attachment (nom. sg. masc., predicate)
action (first member)
fruit (second member)
desirous of obtaining (desiderative adj.; karma-phala-prepsuḥ: 'craving the fruit of action', nom. sg. masc., predicate; -uḥ+l- → -ur l-)
greedy, covetous (nom. sg. masc., predicate; -aḥ before h- → -o)
violence, injury (first member)
having the nature of, characterized by (hiṃsā-ātmakaḥ: 'violent by nature', nom. sg. masc., predicate; -aḥ+a- → -o' with avagraha)
impure, unclean (nom. sg. masc., predicate)
joy, elation (first member)
grief (second member)
possessed by, subject to (harṣa-śoka-anvitaḥ: 'subject to elation and grief', nom. sg. masc., predicate; harṣaśoka+anvitaḥ → harṣaśokānvitaḥ, a+a → ā)
the agent, the doer (nom. sg. masc., subject)
rajas-natured (nom. sg. masc., predicate)
to proclaim (parikīrtita: past participle; nom. sg. masc., predicate)

sentences.l: Passionate, desiring-the-fruit-of-action, greedy, of-a-violent-nature, impure, subject-to-elation-and-grief — [such an] agent is-proclaimed rajas-natured.
sentences.i: An agent who is passionate, craves the fruit of action, is greedy, violent by nature, impure, and subject to elation and grief — such an agent is proclaimed rajas-natured.
sentences.n: The rajas-natured agent: rāgī, 'passionate', karma-phala-prepsuḥ, 'craving the fruit of action', directly opposes verse 26's mukta-saṅgaḥ; lubdhaḥ, 'greedy', hiṃsā-ātmakaḥ, 'violent by nature', aśuciḥ, 'impure', and harṣa-śoka-anvitaḥ, 'given to elation and grief', complete a portrait of an agent wholly at the mercy of circumstance and desire, against verse 26's steadiness in success and failure.

sentences.t:
अयुक्तः प्राकृतः स्तब्धः शठो नैष्कृतिकोऽलसः ।
विषादी दीर्घसूत्री च कर्ता तामस उच्यते ॥
sentences.tr:
ayuktaḥ prākṛtaḥ stabdhaḥ śaṭhaḥ naiṣkṛtikaḥ alasaḥ |
viṣādī dīrgha-sūtrī ca kartā tāmasaḥ ucyate ||

morph.gloss: undisciplined, not joined [in yoga] (nom. sg. masc., predicate)
vulgar, coarse, unrefined (nom. sg. masc., predicate)
stiff, arrogant, obstinate (stabdha: past participle; nom. sg. masc., predicate)
deceitful, crafty, wicked (nom. sg. masc., predicate; -aḥ before n- → -o)

unfaithful, given to fraud, wicked (from niṣkṛti, 'cheating, breach of agreement'; nom. sg. masc., predicate; -aḥ+a- → -o' with avagraha — the vulgate reading, printed here; the BORI critical edition reads naikṛtikaḥ, a close synonym from the related noun nikṛti, 'deceit': a real vulgate/BORI variant, not a misprint; see the note)
lazy, indolent (nom. sg. masc., predicate)
despondent, gloomy, prone to dejection (nom. sg. masc., predicate)
long (first member)
'threaded', i.e. one who draws things out, procrastinating (dīrgha-sūtrī: 'chronically procrastinating', nom. sg. masc., predicate)
and
the agent, the doer (nom. sg. masc., subject)
tamas-natured (nom. sg. masc., predicate; visarga elided before the vowel u- of ucyate, hiatus retained, as at verse 26)
to say (ucyate: present passive 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: Undisciplined, vulgar, obstinate, deceitful, unfaithful, lazy, despondent, and-procrastinating — [such an] agent is-called tamas-natured.
sentences.i: An agent who is undisciplined, coarse, arrogant, deceitful, unscrupulous, lazy, prone to despair, and always putting things off — such an agent is called tamas-natured.
sentences.n: Closes the kartā-triad and, with it, the whole three-triad analysis of verse 19. Vulgate reads naiṣkṛtikaḥ, 'unfaithful, given to fraud' (from niṣkṛti, 'cheating, breach of agreement'); the BORI critical edition reads naikṛtikaḥ, a close synonym from the related noun nikṛti, 'deceit' — a real vulgate/BORI variant, not adopted here but noted. Ayuktaḥ, 'undisciplined', directly opposes verse 26's steadiness; dīrghasūtrī, literally 'long-threaded', a vivid idiom for chronic procrastination, closes the list. The chapter now turns from the components of action (verses 18-28) to a second guṇa-analysis, of buddhi, dhṛti and sukha (verses 29-39).

sentences.t:
बुद्धेर्भेदं धृतेश्चैव गुणतस्त्रिविधं शृणु ।
प्रोच्यमानमशेषेण पृथक्त्वेन धनंजय ॥
sentences.tr:
buddheḥ bhedam dhṛteḥ ca eva guṇataḥ trividham śṛṇu |
procyamānam aśeṣeṇa pṛthaktvena dhanaṃjaya ||

morph.gloss: intellect, understanding (buddheḥ: gen. sg., 'of intellect')
distinction, division (bhedam: acc. sg. masc., object of śṛṇu; -eḥ+bh- → -er bh-)
steadfastness, firmness, resolve (dhṛteḥ: gen. sg., 'of steadfastness'; -eḥ+c- → -eś c-)
and
indeed (ca+eva → caiva, a+e → ai)
guṇa, kept untranslated per convention (guṇataḥ: ablative-adverbial, 'according to guṇa')
threefold (trividham: acc. sg. masc., agreeing with bhedam; simply joined, dental+dental)
to hear (śṛṇu: imperative 2nd sg.)
to be declared (procyamāna: present passive participle; acc. sg. masc., agreeing with bhedam)
completely, fully, without remainder (instr. sg. used adverbially; simply joined, final -m unaffected before the vowel)
separateness, distinctness (instr. sg. used adverbially, 'point by point')
'winner of wealth', an epithet of Arjuna (vocative)

sentences.l: Of-intellect the-distinction, and-of-steadfastness, according-to-guṇa threefold, hear — being-declared fully, separately, Dhanañjaya.
sentences.i: Now hear the threefold division of intellect, and of steadfastness too, according to guṇa, set out fully and point by point, Dhanañjaya.
sentences.n: Introduces the second guṇa-analysis of the chapter's central section: buddhi, 'intellect, discernment' (verses 30-32) and dhṛti, 'steadfastness, resolve' (verses 33-35), each divided sāttvika/rājasa/tāmasa as jñāna, karma and kartā already were (verses 20-28); sukha, 'happiness', receives the same treatment immediately after (verses 36-39). Dhanañjaya, 'winner of wealth', a standing epithet of Arjuna.

sentences.t:
प्रवृत्तिं च निवृत्तिं च कार्याकार्ये भयाभये ।
बन्धं मोक्षं च या वेत्ति बुद्धिः सा पार्थ सात्त्विकी ॥
sentences.tr:
pravṛttim ca nivṛttim ca kārya-akārye bhaya-abhaye |
bandham mokṣam ca yā vetti buddhiḥ sā pārtha sāttvikī ||

morph.gloss: engagement, activity, undertaking (acc. sg. fem., object of vetti)
and
cessation, withdrawal, abstention (acc. sg. fem., object)
and
what is to be done (first item)
what is not to be done (kārya-akārye: acc. dual neut, 'the to-be-done and not-to-be-done'; kārya+akārye → kāryākārye, a+a → ā)
fear (first item)
fearlessness (bhaya-abhaye: acc. dual neut, 'fear and fearlessness'; bhaya+abhaye → bhayābhaye, a+a → ā)
bondage (acc. sg. masc., object)
liberation (acc. sg. masc., object)
and
which (nom. sg. fem. relative, subject)
to know (vetti: present 3rd sg.)
intellect, discernment (nom. sg. fem., subject)
that (nom. sg. fem., correlative)
son of Pṛthā, Arjuna (vocative)
sattva-natured (nom. sg. fem., predicate)

sentences.l: Engagement and cessation, the-to-be-done-and-not-to-be-done, fear and fearlessness, bondage and liberation — which intellect knows, that intellect, Pārtha, [is] sattva-natured.
sentences.i: The intellect that knows engagement and withdrawal, what should and should not be done, fear and fearlessness, bondage and liberation — that intellect, Pārtha, is sattva-natured.
sentences.n: Opens the buddhi-triad (verses 30-32): pravṛtti and nivṛtti, 'engagement [in action]' and 'withdrawal [from it]' (the two orientations weighed since 3.4-8); kārya and akārya, 'what should and should not be done'; bhaya and abhaya, 'fear and fearlessness' (abhaya itself heads the list of divine qualities at 16.1); and bandha and mokṣa, 'bondage and liberation' — six paired opposites whose correct discrimination is exactly what buddhi is for. Sāttvikī buddhi knows all six pairs truly.

sentences.t:
यया धर्ममधर्मं च कार्यं चाकार्यमेव च ।
अयथावत्प्रजानाति बुद्धिः सा पार्थ राजसी ॥
sentences.tr:
yayā dharmam adharmam ca kāryam ca akāryam eva ca |
ayathāvat prajānāti buddhiḥ sā pārtha rājasī ||

morph.gloss: by which (instr. sg. fem. relative, referring to buddhi)
dharma, kept untranslated per convention (dharmam: acc. sg. masc., object of prajānāti)
adharma, kept untranslated per convention (adharmam: acc. sg. masc., object; simply joined, final -m unaffected before the vowel)
and
what is to be done (acc. sg. neut., object)
and (ca+akāryam → cākāryam, a+a → ā)
what is not to be done (akāryam: acc. sg. neut., object)
even, indeed
and
not properly, not as it truly is (adverb)
to discern, understand (prajānāti: present 3rd sg.; simply joined, dental+p, no change)
intellect (nom. sg. fem., subject)
that (nom. sg. fem.)
son of Pṛthā, Arjuna (vocative)
rajas-natured (nom. sg. fem., predicate)

sentences.l: By-which [intellect one] discerns dharma and-adharma, and the-to-be-done and-not-to-be-done, not-properly — that intellect, Pārtha, [is] rajas-natured.
sentences.i: The intellect that discerns dharma and adharma, and what should and should not be done, but not as they truly are — that intellect, Pārtha, is rajas-natured.
sentences.n: The rajas-natured buddhi does not simply fail to discern (that is tamas, verse 32) but discerns ayathāvat, 'not correctly, not as things truly are' — a partial or distorted grasp of dharma and adharma, kārya and akārya, worse than plain ignorance because it passes for genuine understanding.

sentences.t:
अधर्मं धर्ममिति या मन्यते तमसावृता ।
सर्वार्थान्विपरीतांश्च बुद्धिः सा पार्थ तामसी ॥
sentences.tr:
adharmam dharmam iti yā manyate tamasā āvṛtā |
sarva-arthān viparītān ca buddhiḥ sā pārtha tāmasī ||

morph.gloss: adharma, kept untranslated per convention (acc. sg. masc., object of manyate)
dharma, kept untranslated per convention (dharmam: acc. sg. masc., predicate complement; simply joined with iti, final -m unaffected before the vowel)
thus (closing the quoted judgment, 'as dharma')
which (nom. sg. fem. relative, subject)
to think, judge, consider (manyate: present middle 3rd sg.)
tamas, kept untranslated per convention (tamasā: instr. sg. neut., 'by tamas')
covered, enveloped (āvṛtā: past participle; nom. sg. fem., predicate; tamasā+āvṛtā → tamasāvṛtā, ā+ā → ā)

sentences.l: Which, enveloped-by-tamas, judges adharma as-dharma, and all-things as-reversed — that intellect, Pārtha, [is] tamas-natured.
sentences.i: The intellect that, shrouded in tamas, takes adharma to be dharma, and takes everything to be the reverse of what it is — that intellect, Pārtha, is tamas-natured.
sentences.n: Closes the buddhi-triad: tamasā āvṛtā, 'enveloped by tamas' (the same verb used of ignorance covering knowledge at 5.15, 14.8), inverts dharma and adharma outright rather than merely misjudging them (contrast verse 31's ayathāvat), and takes sarva-arthān viparītān, 'all things as their opposite' — total inversion, the lowest of the three.

योगेनाव्यभिचारिण्या धृतिः सा पार्थ सात्त्विकी ॥

sentences.i: The steadfastness by which a person, through yoga, unwaveringly sustains the functions of mind, breath, and senses — that steadfastness, Pārtha, is sattva-natured.
sentences.n: Opens the dhṛti-triad (verses 33-35). Yogena avyabhicāriṇyā, 'through yoga, unwavering' (echoing the unwavering devotion of 13.10's avyabhicāriṇī bhaktiḥ), sustaining manaḥ-prāṇa-indriya-kriyāḥ, 'the functions of mind, breath and the senses' — the full apparatus of the embodied being held steady through disciplined practice, the same picture of yogic self-mastery given at 6.10-14 and echoed later in this chapter's own portrait of the sage (verses 51-53).

sentences.i: But the steadfastness by which a person, out of attachment and craving for reward, holds fast to dharma, pleasure, and wealth, Arjuna — that steadfastness, Pārtha, is rajas-natured.
sentences.n: The rajas-natured resolve fastens not on self-mastery but on dharma-kāma-arthān, the traditional trio of worldly aims (with mokṣa, liberation, as the fourth, cf. verse 30's own bandhaṃ mokṣaṃ), pursued prasaṅgena phala-ākāṅkṣī, 'out of attachment, craving the fruit' — resolve harnessed to desire rather than freed from it.

sentences.l: By-which, sleep, fear, grief, despondency, and-indeed conceit too, [a] dull-witted [person] does-not let-go — that steadfastness, Pārtha, [is] tamas-natured.
sentences.i: The steadfastness, dull-witted as it is, by which a person clings to sleep, fear, grief, despondency, and conceit as well — that steadfastness, Pārtha, is tamas-natured.
sentences.n: Closes the dhṛti-triad: tāmasī dhṛti is not steadiness in any positive practice but sheer inability to let go — svapnam, bhayam, śokam, viṣādam, madam, 'sleep, fear, grief, despondency, conceit', the very afflictions verse 30's sāttvikī buddhi was said to discern rightly, now clung to instead of released. Durmedhā, 'dull-witted', closes the description as durmatiḥ closed the description of the false knower at verse 16.

sentences.t:

sentences.l: But hear from-me now threefold happiness, bull-among-the-Bharatas: wherein [one], through-practice, delights, and reaches the-end-of-suffering,
sentences.i: Now hear from me the three kinds of happiness too, bull among the Bharatas: that in which one comes, through practice, to delight, and reaches the end of suffering —
sentences.n: Opens the third and final guṇa-triad of the chapter's central section, sukha, 'happiness' (verses 36-39), completing the pair begun with buddhi/dhṛti at verse 29. This verse names only the sāttvika type in outline — abhyāsāt ramate, 'comes to delight through practice' (happiness that must be cultivated, not immediate), and duḥkha-antam ... nigacchati, 'reaches the end of suffering' — with its fuller description following in verse 37; bharata-ṛṣabha, 'bull among the Bharatas', an epithet of Arjuna.

sentences.l: That which, at-first, [is] like-poison, [but] in-the-end, like-nectar — that happiness [is] declared sattva-natured, born-of-the-clarity-of-one's-own-understanding.
sentences.i: That happiness which is like poison at first but like nectar in the end — that happiness is declared to be sattva-natured, born of the clarity of one's own understanding.
sentences.n: Completes the sāttvika type of happiness introduced in verse 36 with the chapter's most memorable image: agre viṣam iva, pariṇāme amṛta-upamam, 'like poison at first, like nectar in the end' — happiness that costs effort or discipline up front but ripens into something like amṛta, 'the nectar of immortality'. Ātma-buddhi-prasāda-jam, 'born of the clarity of one's own understanding', names its true source: not external circumstance but an inwardly settled mind (prasāda recalling the serenity already prized at 2.64-65 and 17.16's manaḥ prasādaḥ).

sentences.n: The rajas-natured happiness exactly inverts verse 37's pattern: born of viṣaya-indriya-saṃyogāt, 'the contact of sense-object and sense-organ' (ordinary sensory pleasure, cf. the warning already given at 5.22), it is amṛta-upamam agre, 'like nectar at first', but viṣam iva pariṇāme, 'like poison in the end' — pleasant at the moment of contact but ultimately bitter, the reverse of the sāttvika happiness whose poison-then-nectar order makes it worth the initial cost. The entire first line is one long fused Devanagari token.

sentences.t:

sentences.l: Which happiness, at-first and-thereafter, [is] deluding to-the-self, arisen-from-sleep-laziness-and-negligence — that is declared tamas-natured.
sentences.i: Happiness that deludes the self both at first and in what follows, arising from sleep, laziness, and negligence — that is declared tamas-natured.
sentences.n: Closes the sukha-triad, and with it the whole guṇa-analysis begun at verse 29: unlike verses 37-38's happiness that changes character between beginning and end, tāmasa sukha is mohanam ātmanaḥ, 'deluding to the self', agre ca anubandhe ca, 'both at first and thereafter' — deceptive all the way through, its source named outright as nidrā-ālasya-pramāda, 'sleep, laziness and negligence', echoing tāmasī dhṛti's clinging to sleep at verse 35 and the tamas-natured agent's alasaḥ, 'lazy', at verse 28.

sentences.i: There is no being, on earth or among the gods in heaven, that is free from these three guṇas born of nature.
sentences.n: A transitional summary: after three guṇa-triads (jñāna/karma/kartā, buddhi/dhṛti, sukha), Kṛṣṇa states the premise those triads presuppose — that no sattvam, 'being, entity' (the general sense of the word here, distinct from the guṇa sattva just discussed at length, as already flagged at verse 3 and 17.8), pṛthivyāṃ ... divi deveṣu vā, 'on earth or in heaven among the gods', escapes the three prakṛti-jaiḥ guṇaiḥ, 'guṇas born of nature' (prakṛti as the source of the guṇas, per Sāṃkhya doctrine, e.g. 13.19-21, 14.5). This universal claim sets up the following section (verses 41-48), applying guṇa-based classification to the four varṇas' distinct duties.

sentences.i: The duties of brahmins, kṣatriyas, and vaiśyas, and of śūdras too, scorcher of the foe, are allotted according to the guṇas born of their own nature.
sentences.n: Opens the four-varṇa duty section (verses 41-44), grounding the traditional division of society into brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya and śūdra not in birth as such but in svabhāva-prabhavaiḥ guṇaiḥ, 'the guṇas arising from each person's own nature' — continuing directly from verse 40's claim that all beings are guṇa-bound, and echoing the same grounding of caste in guṇa and karma already given at 4.13 (cātur-varṇyaṃ mayā sṛṣṭaṃ guṇa-karma-vibhāgaśaḥ). sentences.l: Tranquility, self-control, austerity, purity, patience, and-indeed uprightness too, knowledge, discernment, [and] faith — [this is] the-brahmin's-duty, born-of-[his-own]-nature.
sentences.i: Tranquility, self-control, austerity, purity, patience, and uprightness, knowledge, insight, and faith — these, born of his own nature, are the brahmin's duty.
sentences.n: Names the qualities making up brahma-karma, 'the brahmin's duty' — here brahma stands for brāhmaṇa, 'brahmin', not the untranslated metaphysical brahman used elsewhere in the poem, matching the parallel kṣātraṃ karma, vaiśya-karma and śūdrasya karma of verses 43-44. The nine qualities — śama and dama, 'tranquility of mind and control of the senses' (the pair opening the sthitaprajña's portrait at 2.64ff, named again at 10.4), tapas, śauca, kṣānti, ārjava, jñāna, vijñāna, āstikya, 'faith [in scripture and the unseen]' — are dispositions, not birth-marks, again grounded in svabhāvajam, 'born of one's own nature', picking up verse 41's svabhāva-prabhavaiḥ guṇaiḥ.

sentences.t:
शौर्यं तेजो धृतिर्दाक्ष्यं युद्धे चाप्यपलायनम् ।
दानमीश्वरभावश्च क्षात्रं कर्म स्वभावजम् ॥
sentences.tr:

sentences.l: Heroism, vigor, steadfastness, skill, and-even not-fleeing in-battle, generosity, and-a-commanding-disposition — [this is] the-kṣatriya's duty, born-of-[his-own]-nature.
sentences.i: Heroism, vigor, steadfastness, resourcefulness, not fleeing even in battle, generosity, and a commanding presence — these, born of his own nature, are the kṣatriya's duty.
sentences.n: Vulgate reads kṣātraṃ karma, adjective plus noun ('kṣatriya-belonging duty'); the BORI critical edition instead compounds the two as kṣatra-karma, 'kṣatriya-duty', reaching the same sense as one word rather than two — a real vulgate/BORI variant, not adopted here but noted. Śaurya, teja, dhṛti, dākṣya, 'heroism, vigor, steadfastness, resourcefulness', yuddhe ca apy apalāyanam, 'not fleeing even in battle', dāna, 'generosity' (the ruler's traditional virtue of largesse), and īśvara-bhāvaḥ, 'a commanding disposition', complete the portrait of the warrior-and-ruler class's native character, again svabhāvajam, 'born of one's own nature'.

sentences.t:
कृषिगौरक्ष्यवाणिज्यं वैश्यकर्म स्वभावजम् ।
परिचर्यात्मकं कर्म शूद्रस्यापि स्वभावजम् ॥
sentences.tr:
kṛṣi-gau-rakṣya-vāṇijyam vaiśya-karma svabhāvajam |
paricaryā-ātmakam karma śūdrasya api svabhāvajam ||

a cow (here in the vulgate's spelling appearing as the nominative-like gau- before rakṣya rather than the ordinary compounding stem go- — see note)
protection, tending (go-rakṣya: 'cattle-tending')

trade, commerce (kṛṣi-gau-rakṣya-vāṇijyam: 'farming, cattle-tending and trade', nom. sg. neut., subject — the vulgate reading, printed here; the BORI critical edition reads the more regular kṛṣi-go-rakṣya-vāṇijyam, with the ordinary stem go-: a real vulgate/BORI variant in the compound's internal form, not a misprint and not a difference of sense; see the note)
a vaiśya (first member)

action (nom. sg. neut., subject)
a śūdra (śūdrasya: gen. sg., 'of the śūdra')
too, also (śūdrasya+api → śūdrasyāpi, a+a → ā)
one's own nature (first member)
born of (nom. sg. neut., predicate)

sentences.l: Farming, cattle-tending, and trade — [this is] the-vaiśya's-duty, born-of-[his-own]-nature; [and] the-duty consisting-in-service [is] the-śūdra's too, born-of-[his-own]-nature.
sentences.i: Farming, tending cattle, and trade are the vaiśya's duty, born of his own nature; and service is the śūdra's duty as well, born of his own nature.
sentences.n: Closes the four-varṇa section. Vulgate reads kṛṣi-gau-rakṣya-vāṇijyam, using gauḥ (the nominative singular of go, 'cow') itself as a compound member before rakṣya, 'tending'; the BORI critical edition reads the more regular kṛṣi-go-rakṣya-vāṇijyam, with the ordinary compounding stem go- — a real vulgate/BORI variant in the compound's internal form, not a difference of sense ('farming, cattle-rearing and trade' either way), not adopted here but noted. Paricaryā-ātmakam karma, 'duty consisting in service', names the śūdra's role by function (attending on the other three classes) rather than by a list of virtues, unlike the three verses before it; api, 'too, as well', signals that this duty is equally svabhāvajam, 'born of one's own nature' — the section's closing point: all four duties arise from inborn nature rather than external ranking, grounding the argument for the value of one's own duty that follows in verses 45-48.

sentences.t:
स्वे स्वे कर्मण्यभिरतः संसिद्धिं लभते नरः ।
स्वकर्मनिरतः सिद्धिं यथा विन्दति तच्छृणु ॥
sentences.tr:
sve sve karmaṇi abhirataḥ saṃsiddhim labhate naraḥ |
sva-karma-nirataḥ siddhim yathā vindati tat śṛṇu ||

one's own (repeated for a distributive sense, 'each in his own')
action (karmaṇi: loc. sg., 'in [his own] duty')
devoted to, delighting in (abhirata: past participle; nom. sg. masc., predicate; karmaṇi+abhirataḥ → karmaṇyabhirataḥ, -i+a- → -y a-)

to obtain (labhate: present middle 3rd sg.)

own (first member)
action (second member)
devoted to, intent on (nirata: past participle; sva-karma-nirataḥ: 'devoted to his own duty', nom. sg. masc., subject)

how, in what way
to find, obtain (vindati: present 3rd sg.)
that (tat: acc. sg. neut., object of śṛṇu; tat+śṛṇu → tacchṛṇu, -t+ś- → -c ch-)
to hear (śṛṇu: imperative 2nd sg.)

sentences.l: Each-in-his-own duty devoted, accomplishment obtains a-man; devoted-to-his-own-duty, how he-finds accomplishment — that hear.
sentences.i: A person devoted to his own duty attains accomplishment; now hear how one devoted to his own duty finds that accomplishment.
sentences.n: Opens the chapter's return to the value of one's own duty (verses 45-48), the practical conclusion of the guṇa-based analysis of varṇa-duty just given: sve sve karmaṇi abhirataḥ, 'devoted each to his own duty' (whichever of the four just described applies to him), naraḥ saṃsiddhiṃ labhate, 'a person attains accomplishment' — the poem's recurring argument (already made at 3.35, and again below at 18.47) that spiritual success does not require abandoning one's social role, but performing it rightly. The full answer follows in verse 46.

sentences.t:
यतः प्रवृत्तिर्भूतानां येन सर्वमिदं ततम् ।
स्वकर्मणा तमभ्यर्च्य सिद्धिं विन्दति मानवः ॥
sentences.tr:
yataḥ pravṛttiḥ bhūtānām yena sarvam idam tatam |
sva-karmaṇā tam abhyarcya siddhim vindati mānavaḥ ||

morph.gloss: from whom, from which (yataḥ: abl. sg. relative used adverbially)
activity, emanation, coming-forth (pravṛttiḥ: nom. sg. fem., subject; -iḥ+bh- → -ir bh-)
a being (bhūtānām: gen. pl., 'of beings')
by whom (instr. sg. relative)
all (sarvam: nom. sg. neut., subject)
this (idam: nom. sg. neut., in apposition)

own (first member)
action (sva-karmaṇā: 'through his own duty', instr. sg.)
him (tam: acc. sg. masc., object of abhyarcya, referring to the source just named)
to worship, honor (abhyarcya: gerund, 'having worshipped'; simply joined, final -m unaffected before the vowel)
accomplishment (siddhi: acc. sg. fem., object of vindati)
to find, attain (vindati: present 3rd sg.)
a human being, a man (nom. sg. masc., subject)

sentences.l: From-whom [is] the-emanation of-beings, by-whom this-all [is] pervaded — him, through-his-own-duty, having-worshipped, a-man attains accomplishment.
sentences.i: By worshipping, through his own duty, him from whom all beings arise and by whom this whole universe is pervaded, a person attains accomplishment.
sentences.n: Answers verse 45's question by naming the ultimate object of svakarma performed rightly: yataḥ pravṛttir bhūtānām, 'from whom is the emanation of beings' (recalling 7.6, 10.8's ahaṃ sarvasya prabhavaḥ), and yena sarvam idaṃ tatam, 'by whom this whole [universe] is pervaded' (echoing 9.4's mayā tatam idaṃ sarvam) — plainly Kṛṣṇa himself, left here unnamed as tam, 'him'. Sva-karmaṇā tam abhyarcya, 'having worshipped him through his own duty', compresses the whole teaching of karma-yoga (chapters 3-4) into one line: ordinary work, rightly performed, is itself an act of worship.

sentences.t:
श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् ।
स्वभावनियतं कर्म कुर्वन्नाप्नोति किल्बिषम् ॥
sentences.tr:
śreyān sva-dharmaḥ viguṇaḥ para-dharmāt su-anuṣṭhitāt |
svabhāva-niyatam karma kurvan na āpnoti kilbiṣam ||

action (acc. sg. neut., object of kurvan)
doing (kurvant: present participle; kurvan: nom. sg. masc., 'while doing'; kurvan+na simply joined, doubling the n)
not

sentences.l: Better, one's-own-dharma, deficient, than-another's-dharma well-performed: doing the-action determined-by-[one's-own]-nature, one-does-not incur sin.
sentences.i: One's own dharma, imperfectly done, is better than another's dharma well performed; doing the duty set by one's own nature, a person incurs no sin.
sentences.n: Restates the maxim already given at 3.35 (śreyān sva-dharmo viguṇaḥ para-dharmāt sv-anuṣṭhitāt — this first line word for word identical), now placed just after the fourfold varṇa-duty section rather than before Arjuna's own crisis. Sva-dharma, 'one's own dharma' (the duty proper to one's class and inborn nature, as just detailed in verses 41-44), is kept untranslated per convention, in this personal-duty sense distinct from dharma as cosmic order; svabhāva-niyataṃ karma, 'duty fixed by one's own nature', closes the thought with a promise: performing it, whatever its imperfections, incurs no kilbiṣam, 'sin, fault' — the very worry that opened Arjuna's crisis in chapter 1.

sentences.t:
सहजं कर्म कौन्तेय सदोषमपि न त्यजेत् ।
सर्वारम्भा हि दोषेण धूमेनाग्निरिवावृताः ॥

action (acc. sg. neut., object of tyajet)
son of Kuntī, Arjuna (vocative)
with, together with (prefix)
fault, flaw (sa-doṣam: 'though flawed', acc. sg. neut., agreeing with karma; simply joined with api, final -m unaffected before the vowel)

all (first member)
an undertaking, a beginning [of action] (sarva-ārambhāḥ: 'all undertakings', nom. pl. masc., subject; sarva+ārambhāḥ → sarvārambhāḥ, a+ā → ā)

fault, flaw (instr. sg., 'by fault')
smoke (dhūmena: instr. sg.; dhūmena+agniḥ → dhūmenāgniḥ, a+a → ā)
fire (agniḥ: nom. sg. masc., subject of the comparison; -iḥ+i- → -ir i-)

sentences.l: Inborn duty, Kaunteya, though-flawed, one-should-not abandon; for-all undertakings, by-fault, like-fire by-smoke, [are] enveloped.
sentences.i: One should not give up inborn duty, Kaunteya, even though it is flawed; for all undertakings are enveloped by some flaw, as fire is enveloped by smoke.
sentences.n: Closes the argument for sva-dharma (verses 45-48) with a memorable simile: sahajaṃ karma, 'inborn duty' (echoing svabhāva-niyataṃ of verse 47), should not be given up sadoṣam api, 'even though flawed', because sarva-ārambhāḥ, 'all undertakings whatsoever' (not only one's own duty, but any action at all), are doṣeṇa āvṛtāḥ, 'enveloped by some flaw', dhūmena agniḥ iva, 'as fire is enveloped by smoke' — imperfection is simply the price of acting in the world, so it cannot be a reason to abandon one's own duty. This closes the chapter's argument (from verse 41) that duty tied to one's own nature, not renunciation of duty, is the right course, and sets up verse 49's turn to the deeper renunciation available even to one who keeps acting.

sentences.t:
असक्तबुद्धिः सर्वत्र जितात्मा विगतस्पृहः ।
नैष्कर्म्यसिद्धिं परमां संन्यासेनाधिगच्छति ॥
sentences.tr:
asakta-buddhiḥ sarvatra jita-ātmā vigata-spṛhaḥ |
naiṣkarmya-siddhim paramām saṃnyāsena adhigacchati ||

morph.gloss: not attached, unattached (past participle of sañj negated; first member)
intellect (a-sakta-buddhiḥ: 'whose intellect is unattached', nom. sg. masc., subject)
everywhere (adverb)
conquered (jita: past participle; first member)
self (jita-ātmā: 'self-conquered', nom. sg. masc., predicate)
gone away, departed (first member)
longing, craving (vigata-spṛhaḥ: 'from whom craving has departed', nom. sg. masc., predicate)
freedom from the bondage of action, actionlessness (first member)
attainment, perfection (naiṣkarmya-siddhim: 'the perfection of actionlessness', acc. sg. fem., object of adhigacchati)
supreme (acc. sg. fem., agreeing with siddhim)
renunciation (saṃnyāsena: instr. sg., 'through renunciation')
to reach, attain (adhigacchati: present 3rd sg.; saṃnyāsena+adhigacchati → saṃnyāsenādhigacchati, a+a → ā)

sentences.l: Whose-intellect-is-unattached everywhere, self-conquered, free-from-craving — the-supreme perfection-of-actionlessness, through-renunciation, he-attains.
sentences.i: One whose intellect is unattached everywhere, who is self-controlled and free from craving, attains through renunciation the supreme perfection that lies beyond action.
sentences.n: Opens the chapter's return to renunciation proper (verses 49-53), now as an inward state compatible with continued action rather than the outright abstention rejected in verses 3-12. Asakta-buddhiḥ sarvatra, 'whose intellect is unattached everywhere' (echoing the ideal already given at 2.57, 5.10), jitātmā, 'self-conquered', vigata-spṛhaḥ, 'free from craving', attains naiṣkarmya-siddhiṃ paramām, 'the supreme perfection of actionlessness' — naiṣkarmya, a state beyond the bondage of action even while perhaps still acting outwardly (cf. 3.4's naiṣkarmyaṃ) — reached saṃnyāsena, 'through [this kind of] renunciation'.

sentences.t:
सिद्धिं प्राप्तो यथा ब्रह्म तथाप्नोति निबोध मे ।
समासेनैव कौन्तेय निष्ठा ज्ञानस्य या परा ॥
sentences.tr:
siddhim prāptaḥ yathā brahma tathā āpnoti nibodha me |
samāsena eva kaunteya niṣṭhā jñānasya yā parā ||

sentences.l: One-who-has-attained accomplishment, how brahman he-thus-reaches — learn from-me, in-summary-only, Kaunteya: which [is] the-supreme culmination of-knowledge.
sentences.i: Learn from me now, in brief, Kaunteya, how one who has attained that perfection then reaches brahman — the highest culmination of knowledge.
sentences.n: Promises to explain the final step: siddhiṃ prāptaḥ, 'one who has attained [that] perfection' just named (naiṣkarmya-siddhi, verse 49), goes on to reach brahma, 'brahman', kept untranslated per convention. Niṣṭhā jñānasya yā parā, 'the supreme culmination of knowledge', recalls the same word niṣṭhā used to ask about types of faith at 17.1, now naming knowledge's own highest resting-point; the description that follows (verses 51-53) is a compressed portrait of the sage's discipline, comparable to 6.10-14's fuller instructions on meditation.

sentences.t:
बुद्ध्या विशुद्ध्या युक्तो धृत्यात्मानं नियम्य च ।
शब्दादीन्विषयांस्त्यक्त्वा रागद्वेषौ व्युदस्य च ॥

buddhyā viśuddhyā yuktaḥ dhṛtyā ātmānam niyamya ca |
śabda-ādīn viṣayān tyaktvā rāga-dveṣau vyudasya ca ||

steadfastness, firmness, resolve (dhṛtyā: instr. sg., 'with resolve')
the self (ātmānam: acc. sg., object of niyamya; dhṛtyā+ātmānam → dhṛtyātmānam, ā+ā → ā)
to restrain, control (niyamya: gerund, 'having restrained')
and
sound (first member)
and so on (śabda-ādīn: 'sound and the rest [of the sense-objects]', acc. pl. masc., agreeing with viṣayān)
a sense-object (viṣayān: acc. pl. masc., object of tyaktvā; -n+t- → -ṃs t-)
to abandon (tyaktvā: gerund, 'having given up')
attraction, passion (first member)

sentences.l: Endowed with-intellect, with-purity, and having-restrained the-self with-resolve, and having-abandoned sound-and-other sense-objects, and having-cast-away attraction-and-aversion,
sentences.i: Endowed with a pure intellect, restraining himself with resolve, giving up sound and the other sense-objects, and casting away attraction and aversion,
sentences.n: Opens the chapter's closing portrait of the sage who reaches brahman (verses 51-53). Vulgate reads buddhyā viśuddhyā yuktaḥ, treating viśuddhi as a noun standing beside buddhyā ('endowed with intellect, with purity'); the BORI critical edition reads buddhyā viśuddhayā yuktaḥ, with viśuddhayā as an adjective agreeing directly with buddhyā ('endowed with a purified intellect') — a real vulgate/BORI variant, not adopted here but noted; the sense differs only slightly either way. Dhṛtyā ātmānaṃ niyamya, 'restraining the self with resolve', śabdādīn viṣayān tyaktvā, 'giving up sound and the other sense-objects' (the objects of the five senses, named by their first member, as at 15.9's śabda-sparśa-rūpa-rasa-gandhāṃś ca), and rāga-dveṣau vyudasya, 'casting away attraction and aversion' (the same pair analyzed throughout the poem, cf. verse 10) begin a chain of gerunds completed only in verse 53's kalpate.

sentences.t:
विविक्तसेवी लघ्वाशी यतवाक्कायमानसः ।
ध्यानयोगपरो नित्यं वैराग्यं समुपाश्रितः ॥
sentences.tr:
vivikta-sevī laghu-āśī yata-vāk-kāya-mānasaḥ |
dhyāna-yoga-paraḥ nityam vairāgyam samupāśritaḥ ||

resorting to, given to (vivikta-sevī: 'given to solitude', nom. sg. masc., predicate)
light, small (first member)
eating (laghu-āśī: 'eating little', nom. sg. masc., predicate; laghu+āśī → laghvāśī, -u+ā- → -v ā-, yaṇ sandhi)
controlled, restrained (yata: past participle; first member)
speech (second member, surface vāk- before k-)
body (third member)
mind (yata-vāk-kāya-mānasaḥ: 'whose speech, body and mind are controlled', nom. sg. masc., predicate)
meditation (first member)
yoga, kept untranslated per convention (second member)
intent on, given over to (dhyāna-yoga-paraḥ: 'given over to the yoga of meditation', nom. sg. masc., predicate; -aḥ before n- → -o)
